    1 # Service Guide
    2
    3 This guide describes the small Node.js HTTP service in this repository: what each module does, how requests flow through the router, which endpoints exist to
      day, and which building blocks are available but not yet wired in. Everything here uses only the Node.js standard library, so there is no install step and no
       dependency tree to audit; you need a recent Node.js runtime (one with the global `fetch` and `URL`) and nothing else.
    4
    5 ## Contents
    6
    7 - [Overview](#overview)
    8 - [Modules](#modules)
    9 - [Endpoints](#endpoints)
   10 - [Users API](#users-api)
   11 - [Building blocks](#building-blocks)
   12 - [Error format](#error-format)
   13 - [Limits](#limits)
   14 - [Development](#development)
   15 - [Current status](#current-status)
   16
   17 ## Overview
   18
   19 The service is organised as a set of small, single-purpose CommonJS modules. Request handling lives in `routes.js` and `api.js`, which both export a plain `(
      req, res)` function that can be passed straight to `http.createServer`. Shared response formatting lives in `util.js`, and the remaining modules (`store.js`,
       `cache.js`, `queue.js`, `rate.js`, `logger.js`, `validate.js`, `events.js`) are self-contained utilities that do not import each other, so each one can be r
      ead, tested, and replaced on its own without touching the rest of the codebase.
   20
   21 All responses are JSON. Every handler writes its response through the single `json(res, code, body)` helper in `util.js`, which sets the `content-type: appli
      cation/json` header, writes the status code, and serialises the body; keeping that in one place means a future change such as adding a request id header or s
      witching to pretty-printed output in development only has to be made once.
   22
